content.title: Response To Reviewer nBfd [2/2]
content.comment:
**Q3: Qualitative and Quantitative Comparison with other methods**

A3: 
Due to the characteristics of target domain like the fixed mouse pattern in werewolf, there is inevitable diversity loss in the adaptation process. 
The aim of our proposed spectral consistency regularization is to better preserve diversity under the condition of achieving style effects of target domains.
In Table 1, the SCC performs best for diversity metrics but it does poorly for domain adaptation effects as shown in Figure 5.
We analyze the difference between our method and the other two regularization methods MS and Within that are similar to ours in quantitative results of diversity in detail as follows.

In Appendix A.5, we explain the details of other different regularization methods. Specifically, the Mode Seeking(MS) regularization directly 
maximizes the ratio of the distance between $G(z_1)$ and $G(z_2)$ with respect to the distance between $z_1$ and $z_2$, i.e. $L_{ms} = \frac{d_I({\left(G\left(z_1\right), G\left(z_2\right)\right)}}{d_{z}\left(z_1, z_2\right)}$. 
The drawback is that the loss will be very large when the sampled latent codes are close and it will always push away samples even when the diversity between source and target generator is consistent. 
The Within regularization encourages the cosine similarity between the directions of in-domain samples from source and target generator $E_I(G_s(w_1)) - E_I(G_s(w_2))$ 
and $E_I(G_t(w_1)) - E_I(G_t(w_2))$. During adaptation, the target generator will be restricted by the semantic direction in source domain.
These two regularizations are both too strong. For example, for the target domain of werewolf in Figure 5, both MS and Within fail to transfer the "eyes" to gold color.
In comparison, our method is agnostic of the absolute features of source and target samples and builds a direct relation between the diversity of source and target samples, which achieves better fidelity and stylization of target domain.

We provide more comparison results with other regularization methods in Figure 11 of the revised paper. 
It's obvious in Figure 11 that while MS and Within are able to preserve the attributes of source image, 
they often restrict style adaptation too much, especially in the last row that the faces generated by MS and Within are more like photos instead of paintings. 
Different from that, our methods achieve a suitable balance between the effects of adaptation and attribute preservation.

content.title: Response To Reviewer nBfd [1/2]
content.comment:
Thanks for your detailed and constructive review. We appreciate your positive feedback about the motivation and novelty of this paper. The responses to your comments are as follows:

**Q1: The relation between Hessian Trace and Diversity**  
A1: Considering the mapping from standard normal distribution $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ to general multivariate normal distribution $y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ with the generator as a linear function $G(z) = Az + b$, which has $\mu = b, \Sigma = AA^T$. 
The linear assumption of generator holds when we consider a small neighborhood around $z$, i.e. $\lim \Delta z \rightarrow 0$.

The variance of $y$ can be computed as:
$$
\begin{align*}
Var(y) &= E[\| y- E[y] \|^2_2] \\\\
       &=  E[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-E[y_i])^2] \\\\
       &= \sum_{i=1}^n E[(y_i-E[y_i])^2] \\\\
       &= \sum_{i=1}^n Var(y_i) \\\\
       &= \sum_{i=1}^n \Sigma_{ii} \\\\
       &= Trace(\Sigma) = Trace(AA^T)
\end{align*}
$$

On the other side, the $d^2(G(z), G(z+\Delta z))$ can be expanded as follows:
$$
\begin{align*}
d^2(G(z), G(z+\Delta z)) & = \| G(z)-G(z+\Delta z) \|_2^2 \\\\
                         & =  \| Az+b - (A(z+\Delta z) + b)\|_2^2 \\\\
                         & = \|A \Delta z \| \\\\
                         & = \Delta z^T A^T A \Delta z
\end{align*}
$$
such the Hessian Matrix $H$ of $\Delta z$ with respect to $d^2(G(z), G(z+\Delta z))$ equals to $A^TA$, e.g. $H = A^TA$.

Combining above two equations with $Trace(AA^T) = Trace(A^TA)$, we have $Var(y) = Trace(H)$, which means that the Hessian Trace for every sample in target distribution reflects the variance and diversity of this distribution. If the Hessian Trace is small, the target distribution only spans a small region in space. This is consistent to the mode collapse problem in generative models.

Thanks for your advice and we have added above discussion in Appendix A.8 of the revised paper.

**Q2: The adaptive loss reweighting**

A2: Different from the manually predefined hyperparameter, our adaptive loss weight is a dynamic value according to the gradient from the two loss terms for each iteration during training. 
Specifically, after we calculate the two loss items ${L_{reg}}$ and ${L_{spectral}}$ in the forward pass, we backward twice for each loss item separately and at each time we only calculate the gradient of last layer of generator with respect to one loss item. 
Then we backward the reweighed loss item 
$$ 
L = L_{dir} + \lambda_{spectral} \frac{ \| \nabla_{G_L} L_{dir} \| } { \| \nabla_{G_L} L_{reg} \| } L_{reg}
$$ 
and calculate the gradient for the whole generator, where $\lambda_{spectral}$ is the user-defined hyperparameter for further control.

There are two benefits of this adaptive loss reweighting. First, during each training iteration, it will balance and stabilize the influence of these two loss items by adjusting the gradient of generator with respect to each loss item. 
Second, it helps set an appropriate initial loss weight for different target domains. 
The gradient magnitude for directional loss $L_{dir}$ varies with the domain gap between source and target domain. A fixed hyperparameter can't handle all different domains. 
With the help of the adaptive loss reweighting, the $\lambda_{spectral}$ works better for different target domains.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ekfs
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to carefully review our paper and giving advice. The response to your question is as follows:

**Q1: Comparison to Previous work (Wang & Ponce 2021)**

A1: Related to our work, Wang & Ponce (2021) also exploit the generative models from the geometric point of view. We both leverage the Hessian Matrix to analyze the characteristic of generative models. Here we explain the differences between these two works in detail. First, the aim of Wang & Ponce (2021) is to find interpretable directions in GAN latent space. It can be grouped into the task of unsupervised GAN editing which also includes GANSpace (Härkönen et al. 2020) and SeFa(Shen & Zhou 2021). Instead, we try to solve the mode collapse problem in generative domain adaptation with spectral consistency regularization. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to deploy Hessian Matrix to the domain adaptation problem. Second, Wang & Ponce (2021) leverage the top eigenvectors in Hessian Matrix to find the interpretable directions, while what we utilize is the trace norm of Hessian Matrix to represent the diversity of target generator. The trace norm of Hessian Matrix is agnostic of eigenvectors for both source and target generators and reflects the diversity across all directions. Third, Wang & Ponce (2021) use Lanczos iteration for numerical calculation of top eigenvectors, but our work use Hutchinson’s method to estimate the trace norm.

We have revised our paper and included the above discussion in the Appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fiDS [2/2]
content.comment:
**Q4: Hyperparameter Tuning and Reproducibility**

A4: The spectral consistency regularization only brings one additional hyperparameter $\lambda_{spectral}$ about loss weight beyond baseline model. Further, with the adaptive loss weighting as shown in last paragraph of Section 3.3 in paper, there is no need to exhaustedly tune $\lambda_{spectral}$. Actually, all the figures in our paper were generated with the default hyperparameters as shown in Appendix A.1.
We will also release our code and trained models on Github after the final decision.

**Q5: Typos and Grammar Mistakes**

A5: Thanks for your careful review, we have reexamined our paper and fixed typos and grammar mistakes in the revised version.

**Q6: Generalization of our proposed method**

We propose the spectral consistency regularization to leverage the Hessian Trace of generator to preserve the diversity for generative domain adaptation and have shown its effectiveness on a wide range of target domains. 
Beyond the proposed spectral consistency regularization for domain adaptation, as a general measure of diversity, the Hessian Trace can also be used for other generative tasks like text-to-image synthesis. 
We will explore its effectiveness to other generative tasks in the future work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fiDS [1/2]
content.comment:
Thanks for your detailed reviews and valuable comments. The responses to your questions are as follows:

**Q1 & Q2: Qualitative and Quantitative Comparison with other Methods**

A1 & A2: 
In Appendix A.5, we explain the details of other different regularization methods. Specifically, the Mode Seeking(MS) regularization directly 
maximizes the ratio of the distance between $G(z_1)$ and $G(z_2)$ with respect to the distance between $z_1$ and $z_2$, i.e. $L_{ms} = \frac{d_I({\left(G\left(z_1\right), G\left(z_2\right)\right)}}{d_{z}\left(z_1, z_2\right)}$. 
The drawback is that the loss will be very large when the sampled latent codes are close and it will always push away samples even when the diversity between source and target generator is consistent. 
The Within regularization encourages the cosine similarity between the directions of in-domain samples from source and target generator $E_I(G_s(w_1)) - E_I(G_s(w_2))$ 
and $E_I(G_t(w_1)) - E_I(G_t(w_2))$. During adaptation, the target generator will be restricted by the semantic direction in source domain.
These two regularizations are both too strong. For example, for the target domain of werewolf in Figure 5, both MS and Within fail to transfer the "eyes" to gold color.
In comparison, our method is agnostic of the absolute features of source and target samples and builds a direct relation between the diversity of source and target samples, which achieves better fidelity and stylization of target domain.

We provide more comparison results with other regularization methods in Figure 11 of the revised paper. 
It's obvious in Figure 11 that while MS and Within are able to preserve the attributes of source image, 
they often restrict style adaptation too much, especially in the last row where the faces generated by MS and Within are more like photos instead of paintings. 
Different from that, our methods achieve a suitable balance between the effects of adaptation and attribute preservation.

The quantitative metrics only represent the diversity instead of the overall quality of target generator, due to no groundtruth images of target domain for reference.
On the basis of better performance in the style effects of domain adaptation, we also achieve competitive diversity metrics with the strict regularization methods including MS and Within as shown in Table 1, 

**Q3: Explanation of the choice of input space**

A3: Denote the mapping network $\mathcal Z \rightarrow \mathcal W$ as $f(z; \theta)$, the synthesis network $\mathcal W \rightarrow \mathcal I$ as $g(w; \phi)$, the generator network can be seen as $g(f(z; \theta); \phi)$. Derived from Equation 3 in paper and the chain rule, the Hessian matrix of generator can be calculated as $H_{g \cdot f} = (J_{g} J_{f})^T(J_g J_f) = J_f^T (J_g^TJ_g)J_f = J_f^T H_g J_f$. There are two choices for spectral consistency regularization, which are $H_{g \cdot f}$ and $H_g$. We find regularizing $H_{g}$ is unstable and easily causes artifacts since the density of W space is not ensured compared to Z space as a standard normal distribution. 

As shown in Equation 6 in paper, we use Jacobian-Vector product operation to estimate the Hessian Trace. Since the mapping network is frozen during training, we precompute $e=J_fv$ (e.g. not create compute graph for backpropagation) and only optimize $e^TJ_g^TJ_ge$ during backpropagation.

In the image sampling process, there involves the style-mixing technique, which feeds concatenated w codes generated from different z codes to the synthesis network. 
To integrate this technique, we use W+ space instead of W space for spectral consistency regularization. Furthermore, the W+ space provides the ability for granularity adaptive regularization as shown in Section 3.4 of the paper.

In summary, we regularize the Hessian Matrix $g(f(z; \theta); \phi)$ with respect to z. Compared to Z+ space, we use W+ space for Jacobian-Vector product optimization to avoid overhead compute costs brought by the mapping network during training.
Thanks for your advice. We have revised our paper for better readability.
